system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You are a 42-year-old man. You were admitted to {organization} on December 26, 2021, through the emergency department. You came on your own (self-referral) and stayed in the ward for 23 hours. Your hospital care was covered by SUS.

You have Crohn's disease (a long-term condition that causes inflammation in your digestive system). You were admitted because of abdominal sepsis (a serious infection in your belly) which was linked to acute on chronic kidney disease (meaning your kidneys, which already had a long-term problem, suddenly got worse). Recently, you had an operation called an ileocolectomy (where a part of your small intestine called the ileum and a part of your large intestine called the colon were removed) and a new anastomosis (a new connection was made between the remaining parts of your intestines). This surgery was done because you had an acute perforative abdomen (a sudden hole in your belly, likely in your intestines). You were admitted today to a special monitored bed in the 'red room' because you had hypotension (low BP), fever, and had been fainting (losing consciousness) for one day.

You were recently in [organization] for treatment of an intra-abdominal collection (a build-up of fluid inside your belly), increased urinary output via ileostomy (more urine coming out through your ileostomy, which is a surgically created opening in your belly to allow waste to leave your body), and worsening of renal function (your kidney function getting worse). You were discharged on November 15 with a plan to take ertapenem (an antibiotic to fight infection) 1 gram every day, given as an injection into your muscle, for 4 weeks.

When you were checked, your blood pressure (BP) was borderline (meaning it was on the lower side of normal). A normal BP is usually around 120/80 mmHg. You were eupneic on room air (meaning you were breathing normally without needing any extra oxygen). At the time of the check-up, you said you had no complaints. You reported that you were passing urine normally (physiological diuresis) and that your ostomy (the opening in your belly) was working well.

You were started on antibiotic therapy (treatment with medicines to fight bacterial infections) using vancomycin and meropenem. Vancomycin is an antibiotic used for serious bacterial infections. Meropenem is another antibiotic used for severe bacterial infections. After this, you were moved to the intensive care unit (ICU) of [organization], where you were looked after by the proctology team (doctors who specialize in problems of the colon, rectum, and anus). You were accepted by [person] from the intensive care unit, {omitted}. You continued to receive meropenem and vancomycin (both antibiotics for infection). You also received replacement of KCl 6% orally (potassium chloride, a salt given by mouth to replace potassium in your body, which is important for heart and muscle function). Your ongoing medicines included loperamide (to help with loose motions), calcium carbonate (a medicine for calcium deficiency or to reduce stomach acid), cholestyramine (a medicine to lower cholesterol and help with certain digestive issues), and muciloid (likely a fiber supplement to help with bowel movements).

On December 27, 2021, you were discharged from the hospital. You have a follow-up appointment and are scheduled for another hospitalization on January 22.
